\chapter{El Contrato}
\label{ch:es-trato}
\hlchaptermodality{441}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read the four pieces of paper that decide where my money goes: what I agreed to, that I agreed to it, what I owe, and what I owe it on.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el contrato]{el contrato — drawn together}

\label{lesson:ES-C441-contrato}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el trabajo} and \textbf{el documento}. One document turns a job into an obligation on both sides. Name it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el contrato}
\textbf{el contrato} — the contract.

\emph{Un contrato de trabajo} is an employment contract; \emph{un contrato de alquiler} is a tenancy agreement. The verb is \textbf{contratar}, to hire or to contract: \emph{me han contratado} — they have hired me.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{con-} together, plus \textbf{-trat-} from Latin \textbf{trahere}, to pull or draw.

A contract is \textbf{a drawing-together} — two parties pulled into the same agreement. English says the same thing and has stopped hearing it: \emph{contract}, and also \emph{contraction}, which is a muscle drawing itself in.

\emph{Trahere} is busy in Spanish too. \textbf{traer} is to bring, to draw something to you; \textbf{atraer} is to attract; \textbf{contraer} is to contract a debt or an illness, the same word as the noun above with its verb ending still on.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el contrato}
  \item they have hired me, I have an employment contract
  \item what the two pieces of the word mean
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The contract? (\textbf{El contrato}.) What does \textbf{-trat-} mean? (\textbf{To draw, to pull}.) The verb? (\textbf{Contratar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[firmar]{firmar — to make it firm}

\label{lesson:ES-C441-firmar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el nombre}, \textbf{escribir} and \textbf{el contrato}. Writing your name at the bottom of one of those is not the same act as writing it at the top.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: firmar}
\textbf{firmar} — to sign. \textbf{la firma} — the signature, and also \emph{a firm} in the business sense.

\emph{Firme aquí, por favor} — sign here, please. \emph{Sin firmar} — unsigned, the state a form is in when the clerk hands it back to you.

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{firmus}, firm, solid, not moving. To \textbf{firmar} is \textbf{to make firm}.

The name at the bottom is not information; it is the act that hardens a piece of paper from a proposal into an obligation. Spanish says that outright, where English borrowed \emph{sign} from \emph{signum}, a mark, and kept only the mark.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the word} & \textbf{what it is built on} \\
\midrule
firmar & \emph{firmus}, firm \\
to sign & \emph{signum}, a mark \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English has \emph{firmus} too, in \textbf{firm}, \textbf{affirm} and \textbf{confirm} — all of them about making something hold.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Look at what the two words in this chapter are doing so far.

\textbf{Contrato} draws the parties together. \textbf{Firmar} makes the result solid. They are two halves of one physical picture: pull the sides in, then set them.

That picture is why \textbf{la firma} can also mean a company. A firm is a name that has been made firm — an entity that holds, that you can sign with and be bound by. Spanish did not need a second word for it, and the double meaning is not a coincidence you have to memorise.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{firmar}, then \emph{la firma}
  \item sign the contract here, please
  \item why a company can be called \emph{una firma}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To sign? (\textbf{Firmar}.) The signature? (\textbf{La firma}.) What does \emph{firmus} mean? (\textbf{Firm, solid}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fijo]{fijo — nailed down}

\label{lesson:ES-C441-fijo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la empresa} and \textbf{firmar}. A company offers you two kinds of contract, and only one of them ends on a date.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fijo}
\textbf{fijo} — fixed, permanent, settled.

\emph{Un contrato fijo} is a permanent contract, the one a Spanish job advert contrasts with \emph{temporal}. \emph{Un precio fijo} is a fixed price. \emph{Un cliente fijo} is a regular. The verb is \textbf{fijar}, to fix or to set: \emph{fijar una fecha} — to set a date.

It agrees: \emph{fijo}, \emph{fija}, \emph{fijos}, \emph{fijas}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{fīgere}, to drive in, to fasten — the verb for putting a stake in the ground. \textbf{Fijo} is its past participle, worn down: \emph{the thing that has been fastened}.

English took the same participle intact as \textbf{fix}, and kept the original sense in \textbf{transfix}, to pin something through.

So the chapter now has three ways of binding, and they are all physical:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the picture} \\
\midrule
contrato & pulled together \\
firmar & made solid \\
fijo & driven in \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{cerrado} is a participle you can still feel as one: \emph{cerrar} is right there, and nobody would call \emph{cerrado} a plain adjective.

\textbf{fijo} is a participle too, and nothing about it feels like one. The verb \emph{fijar} exists, but it was built backwards \emph{from} the adjective rather than the other way round, and the form you would expect — \emph{fijado} — also exists and means something narrower.

That is what age does. A participle used constantly enough stops being read as the result of an action and becomes a quality in its own right. \textbf{Cerrado} is still at the first stage; \textbf{fijo} finished the journey centuries ago.

When you meet a short adjective ending in a bare vowel where a verb also exists — \emph{fijo}, \emph{limpio}, \emph{seco} — it is worth asking which came first. The answer is often not the one the modern shape suggests.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{fijo}, then \emph{fija}
  \item I signed a permanent contract
  \item what \emph{fijar una fecha} means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Permanent? (\textbf{Fijo}.) What did \emph{fīgere} mean? (\textbf{To drive in, to fasten}.) The verb built from it? (\textbf{Fijar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la factura]{la factura — a making, itemised}

\label{lesson:ES-C441-factura}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{pagar}, \textbf{la cuenta} and \textbf{el precio}. In a restaurant you ask for \emph{la cuenta}. For work done on a \textbf{contrato}, the paper has a different name.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la factura}
\textbf{la factura} — the invoice, the bill.

\emph{La factura de la luz} — the electricity bill. \emph{¿Me hace una factura?} — could you make me out an invoice? The verb is \textbf{facturar}, to invoice, and also to check in luggage at an airport.

\textbf{la cuenta} is what you ask for at a table; \textbf{la factura} is the formal document, with a number on it, that a business issues and a tax office may want to see.

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{facere}, to make or do, plus \textbf{-tūra}, an ending that names \textbf{the thing an action produces}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{the thing it produces} \\
\midrule
facere, to make & \textbf{factura}, a making \\
escribir, to write & escritura, a writing \\
leer, to read & lectura, a reading \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A \emph{factura} is literally \textbf{a making} — the itemised account of what was made or done for you. The ending is still productive, so when you meet an unfamiliar noun in \textbf{-ura}, look for the verb inside it before you look it up.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\emph{Facere} is one of the two or three hardest-working roots in the language, and you can see it under a lot of words that do not look related.

\textbf{hacer} is its direct Spanish descendant — \emph{facere} lost its \textbf{f} to an \textbf{h} the way \emph{filius} became \emph{hijo}. \textbf{satisfacer} is \emph{satis} plus \emph{facere}, to make enough. \textbf{fácil} is what can be done.

So \emph{la factura} and \emph{hacer} are the same word arriving by different routes: one worn smooth by a thousand years of speech, one lifted off the page by clerks who needed a formal noun. That is the same doublet shape as \textbf{nadar} and \textbf{la natación} — and, as there, the learned twin is the one on the official paper.

A \textbf{precio fijo} and a \textbf{factura} belong to the same world: both are things written down so they stop moving.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la factura}
  \item I have to pay the electricity bill
  \item the difference between \emph{la cuenta} and \emph{la factura}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The invoice? (\textbf{La factura}.) What does the ending \textbf{-ura} name? (\textbf{The thing an action produces}.) Which everyday verb is its worn-down twin? (\textbf{Hacer}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el préstamo]{el préstamo — what lending leaves behind}

\label{lesson:ES-C441-prestamo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{prestar}, \textbf{el banco} and \textbf{el dinero}. You have the verb for handing something over. Name the thing that exists afterwards.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el préstamo}
\textbf{el préstamo} — the loan.

\emph{Pedir un préstamo} — to apply for a loan. \emph{Devolver el préstamo} — to pay it back, with the same \textbf{devolver} the lending cycle already gave you.

The stress is three syllables from the end — \textbf{PRÉS-ta-mo} — and the written accent is what tells you so. Without it the word would be read \emph{pres-TA-mo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
It is \textbf{prestar} with a noun ending, and both go back to Latin \textbf{praestāre} — \emph{prae-} in front, plus \emph{stāre}, to stand. To \emph{praestāre} was \textbf{to stand out in front of} someone: to furnish, to supply, to put something forward.

So a \textbf{préstamo} is what has been \emph{put forward}, and English keeps the same idea in \textbf{to advance} a sum.

This completes a set you already had. \textbf{Prestar} hands it over, \textbf{recoger} fetches it, \textbf{devolver} brings it back — and now \textbf{el préstamo} is the name of the thing while it is out of your hands.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Préstamo} has a second life worth knowing, because you will meet it in this kind of explanation rather than at a bank.

\emph{Un préstamo lingüístico} is a \textbf{loanword} — a word one language has taken from another. Spanish calls \textbf{garaje} and \textbf{sofá} \emph{préstamos}, and it uses the borrowing metaphor exactly as English does, down to the fact that nobody gives them back.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the word on the page} & \textbf{what it is a loan of} \\
\midrule
un préstamo del banco & dinero \\
un préstamo del francés & una palabra \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is the sense in which \textbf{factura} is not a \emph{préstamo} and \textbf{garaje} is: \emph{factura} was taken from the Latin that Spanish itself grew out of, which makes it an inheritance claimed late rather than a borrowing from a neighbour.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el préstamo}
  \item I asked the bank for a loan and I am paying it back
  \item what \emph{un préstamo del francés} means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The loan? (\textbf{El préstamo}.) Which syllable is stressed? (\textbf{The third from the end}.) What did \emph{praestāre} mean? (\textbf{To stand out in front, to furnish}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(contrato, firmar, fijo, factura …]{(contrato, firmar, fijo, factura, préstamo) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R441-repaso-trato}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all five: \emph{the contract}, \emph{to sign}, \emph{permanent}, \emph{the invoice}, \emph{the loan}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: paperwork is a set of physical acts}]
Nothing in this chapter began as an abstraction. Every one of the three binding words is a thing done with the hands.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the act underneath} \\
\midrule
\textbf{contrato} & pull the two sides together \\
\textbf{firmar} & make the result solid \\
\textbf{fijo} & drive it in so it cannot move \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read a Spanish contract with those three in mind and the vocabulary stops looking like jargon. \emph{Contratar}, \emph{firmar}, \emph{fijar} — draw, harden, fasten. The law borrowed its whole vocabulary from carpentry and rope.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I signed a permanent contract with the company
  \item I asked for a loan and I have to pay it back
  \item could you make me out an invoice
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You can now read the four pieces of paper that decide where your money goes} — what you agreed to, that you agreed to it, what you owe, and what you owe it on. That is the administrative half of living somewhere, and it is what an A2 reading paper is mostly made of.

You also have two endings that keep paying. \textbf{-ura} names the thing an action produces, so \emph{factura}, \emph{escritura} and \emph{lectura} stop being three separate words to learn. And \textbf{fijo} showed that a participle used long enough stops feeling like one at all.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The invoice? (\textbf{La factura}.) The contract? (\textbf{El contrato}.) The loan? (\textbf{El préstamo}.) Which everyday verb is \emph{factura}'s worn-down twin? (\textbf{Hacer}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(una oferta de trabajo) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C441-sintesis-trato}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el contrato} and \emph{fijo}. The advert you are about to read uses both, and the second one is the part that matters.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read both, then answer.

\textbf{1 — oferta de empleo}

\begin{quote}
Se busca ayudante de cocina. \textbf{Contrato fijo} a partir de enero, jornada completa. Se valora experiencia previa. Enviar currículum a empleo@cocinacentral.invalid.
\end{quote}

\textbf{2 — un aviso del banco}

\begin{quote}
Le recordamos que la cuota de su \textbf{préstamo} se cargará el día 5. Puede descargar la \textbf{factura} del mes en su área privada. Cualquier cambio de cuenta debe comunicarse \textbf{firmado}.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what kind of contract the job offers, and from when
  \item which of the two documents you would have to sign
  \item what the bank will do on the fifth
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
Notice the last line of the second notice: \textbf{debe comunicarse firmado}.

There is no \emph{you} in it. \textbf{Comunicarse} drains out the person exactly as \emph{celebrarse} did on the notice about the meeting, and \textbf{firmado} is the participle doing an adjective's work, the way \emph{cerrado} does on a shop door. The sentence says \emph{any change must be communicated in-a-signed-state}, and names nobody at all.

That impersonal shape is the register of official Spanish, and it is worth recognising rather than translating. When a notice stops naming who must act, it is not being vague — it is saying the obligation attaches to the \emph{document}, not to a particular clerk.

Contrast the job advert: \emph{se busca}, \emph{se valora}, \emph{enviar}. Same move. An advert and a bank notice are written by the same hand.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Five sentences: say you applied, say what contract you were offered, say you signed it, say you have a loan to pay, and say when the bill arrives.

Then check yourself: did \textbf{fijo} agree with \emph{contrato}, and did you use \textbf{pedir} with \emph{préstamo} rather than \emph{preguntar}?
\end{tcolorbox}
